newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries close higher on weak economic data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries close higher on weak economic data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury securities prices closed sharply higher on Thursday as indicators showed the U.S. economy slowing to a more sustainable rate of growth.

The value of fixed-income securities decline when inflation grows. Thursday's data showed a significant decline in economic activity as retail sales fell for the third consecutive month and initial unemployment claims remained at higher levels -- suggesting the torid pace of growth seen in the fourth quarter of last year and first quarter of 1997 was beginning to subside.
Commerce Department officials noted that retail sales fell for three consecutive months for the first time in 15 years.
Bond market participants had little reaction this session to Treasury Secretary Robert Rubins's comments that excessive volatility in currency markets was "undesirable."

"The retail sales number was the big thing," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc. He said (retail sales) provided an additional reason for investors to continue to buy fixed-income securities. Economic data seen over the past week have been favorable to the bond market.
Iggo said a lot of cash had been sitting on the sidelines and the current economic environment was conducive for buying Treasuries.

"We see GDP growth of 2.0 percent and possibly even less in the second quarter," Iggo said. However, he said strikes at automobile assembly plants and flooding in the Midwest probably impacted growth and a bounceback was likely.
Strength in the Treasury market supported the stock market where the Dow Jones Industrial Average saw hearty gains again, advancing xx points, a historic high.

The bond market liked retail sales data, enough so to be convinced the Federal Reserve would vote not to further tighten monetary policy at its next meeting in July, said Carol Stone, senior economist at Nomura Securities International Inc.
The policy-making Federal Open Market Committee raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points at its March 25 meeting but did not act at its meeting in May.
"We're never in favor of sluggish economic activity. But the data convinced us the Fed won't move in July," Stone said. It also reduced the threat of inflation, she said.
Stone said GDP could slow to 1.0 to 1.5 percent in the second quarter, following the feverish 5.8 percent gain seen in the first quarter -- the strongest since the final quarter of 1987.

"The rest of the story will have to be played out the rest of the month (in official statistics)," Stone said. But, she said, few economists expected a sustained slowdown with unemployment at current low levels and a strong economy.
"Nobody thinks this is the beginning of a collapse. The weather and paying of taxes" in April likely had a strong effect on retail sales, she said.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond ended at 98-6/32, up 30/32, yielding 6.77 percent.

Two-year notes ended at 100-11/32, up 7/32 to yield 6.06 percent. Five-year notes rose 16/32 to 100-21/32 to yield 6.34 percent and the 10-year note was up 22/32 to 101-2/32, its yield at 6.48 percent.
Three-month bill rates fell one basis point to 4.83 percent, six-month rates were down seven basis points at 5.13 percent and year bill rates were off 10 basis points at 5.35 percent.
